I can’t really tell what counts.\n\nDoctor: Do you remember the whole time at the warehouse clearly, or are there parts that feel blank or missing?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d say blank. The boxes were in front of me and then they were in different spots, and someone was saying my name, I think. Or maybe they said “hey” and I thought it was my name. The warehouse has so many sounds that it’s hard to separate them, like when a pallet jack squeaks and then the lights hum and then you start thinking about how the aisles are numbered wrong because they skip—\n\nSorry. I don’t know. I remember some of it, but not clearly all the way through.\n\nDoctor: Did you have a seizure, head injury, or high fever shortly before this happened?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so… I mean, seizure like falling down shaking? Nobody told me that happened. Head injury, I don’t remember hitting my head, but at the warehouse there’s always stuff sticking out, metal edges and pallets, and sometimes you get little bumps and don’t think about it.\n\nHigh fever… I don’t know. I wasn’t taking my temperature or anything. My room gets really hot sometimes because the vent is weird, so you wake up sweating and it’s hard to tell if that’s being sick or just the apartment. But I don’t remember being, like, sick with a fever right before.\n\nDoctor: While this was happening, did it feel like something outside you was controlling your body?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure what you mean by outside me. Like… controlled controlled? I remember my body felt kind of like it was doing things before I was thinking them, but that happens when you’re stressed, right? Like at work when the buzzer goes off and everyone moves at once, you just move.\n\nIt didn’t feel like… I don’t know. Not like a remote control or something. But everything was loud and people were staring, and then I was trying to stand still, or maybe I thought I was standing still. I keep thinking about the way the lights flicker in that place, because if you look up too long it makes your eyes feel weird.\n\nSo… I don’t know if I’d call it something outside controlling me. I can’t really tell.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: I don’t… I don’t know. Like, voices meaning somebody talking clear, like standing behind me? I don’t think so. The forklifts make that backing-up sound and then the radio cuts in, and it’s hard to tell what’s what. So… I haven’t really noticed voices when no one is there, I guess. I’m not sure.\n\nDoctor: When you froze at work with your arms up, were you unable to move even though you wanted to?\n\nPatient: I mean… yeah, I guess? The lights, the beeping, someone telling me to move faster—actually, the way the pallets get wrapped wrong drives me crazy because then they wobble, and everybody acts like it’s your fault even if you weren’t the one who wrapped it.\n\nBut no, I don’t think there was some huge upsetting thing right before. I can’t remember anything like that.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe anyone is trying to harm you or send you special messages?\n\nPatient: I don’t… I’m not sure. Like, harm me how? Sometimes signs or stuff on the radio feel like they’re sticking in my head, but I don’t know if that means anything. There’s this one safety poster by the time clock with the guy pointing, and I always notice it because the finger is drawn weird, like too long, and then I start thinking about who made it and why they picked that color. But that’s not really a message, I guess.\n\nSo… no, I don’t think anyone is trying to send me messages or hurt me. Not that I know of.\n\nDoctor: When someone moved your arms into a new position during that episode, did they stay there?\n\nPatient: I don’t really know if they stayed there because I wasn’t… tracking it right. They told me later people were moving my arms or trying to get me to put them down, but what I remember more is standing by the forklift with my arms up, and the beeping kept catching in my head.\n\nI was copying the beeps and some of the hand signals, I think, and then with the boxes I kept making these little patterns instead of stacking them how they wanted. Everybody was yelling, but it was like the yelling was behind glass or something.\n\nSo… maybe my arms did stay there for a bit? I can’t say it cleanly. That’s part of why they brought me in, I guess, because I kept doing weird stuff like that at the warehouse.\n\nDoctor: As a child, did other kids often say you were odd or hard to understand socially?\n\nPatient: I don’t really know. Kids say a lot of stuff, you know? Like one day they call you weird because your shoes are wrong, next day it’s because you know the answer too fast or you don’t want to play basketball.\n\nI remember more like… lunch tables were hard to figure out, but I don’t know if people said I was hard to understand. There was this one kid who used to chew on the strings of his hoodie, and everyone acted like that was normal, but if I didn’t laugh at the right time then suddenly I was the weird one. It didn’t make sense to me.\n\nSo… maybe sometimes? I’m not sure. I don’t remember it as a big thing people told me directly.\n\nDoctor: Before this warehouse incident, had your ability to work or take care of yourself been getting worse over the past several months?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I guess it was getting worse.
